title: John in 21 Days
subtitle: One chapter a day with the beloved disciple
about: Read the Gospel of John one chapter a day for three weeks, from 'In the beginning was the Word' to breakfast on the shore. Along the way you will meet John's signs, his 'I am' sayings, and the people whose encounters with Jesus changed them. You will come away understanding why John says he wrote: that readers might believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name.

days.title: The Word Became Flesh
days.focus: John begins before creation and then brings the eternal Word into human history. Notice the titles given to Jesus through the chapter: the Word, the Lamb of God, the Messias, the Son of God, the King of Israel.
days.context: John's opening words echo Genesis 1, 'In the beginning.' The idea of a divine 'word' would have meant something to Jewish readers (God's creative speech) and to Greek thinkers (the reason that orders the world) alike.

word.why: John calls Jesus 'the Word' who was with God and was God (v. 1), and who 'was made flesh, and dwelt among us' (v. 14). God's self-expression became a human being.

questions.q: What does John the Baptist call Jesus when he sees him coming (v. 29)?
What does it mean that the Word 'was made flesh, and dwelt among us' (v. 14)?
Which title for Jesus in this chapter means the most to you right now, and why?

checkIn.q: How did John the Baptist describe himself?
options: As the voice of one crying in the wilderness

checkIn.q: Who brought his brother Simon to Jesus?

days.title: Water into Wine
days.focus: Two scenes: a wedding in Cana and the clearing of the temple. Notice what each one shows about Jesus, and how the disciples respond to both.
days.context: Weddings could last several days, and running out of wine would bring public shame on the host family. John places the temple clearing early in Jesus' ministry while the other Gospels place it in his last week; scholars differ on whether this was a second event or John arranged his material by theme.

word.why: John calls the wine at Cana 'this beginning of miracles' (v. 11), using the word for a sign. In John, miracles are signs that point beyond themselves to who Jesus is, and the Gospel is built around them.

questions.q: What did Jesus tell the servants to do with the waterpots?
When Jesus spoke of raising 'this temple' in three days, what does John say he meant (v. 21)?
Where have you seen God provide quietly, in a way only a few people noticed?

checkIn.q: Where was the wedding?
What did Jesus make out of small cords in the temple?

days.title: Born from Above
days.focus: Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night and hears that he must be born again. Notice how the conversation widens into the famous words about God's love, and then closes with John the Baptist's last testimony.
days.context: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and 'a ruler of the Jews,' likely a member of the ruling council. Jesus' reference to Moses lifting up the serpent recalls Numbers 21, where Israelites who looked at a bronze serpent lived.

word.why: This word can mean either 'again' or 'from above' (v. 3). Nicodemus hears 'again' and pictures a second physical birth, but Jesus speaks of a birth from God by the Spirit; both senses fit.

questions.q: What does Nicodemus ask when Jesus says a man must be born again?
According to verses 17–19, why did God send his Son, and why do some people refuse the light?
Like Nicodemus coming 'by night,' what questions about Jesus do you carry quietly?

checkIn.q: When did Nicodemus come to Jesus?
What did John the Baptist say about Jesus?
options: He must increase, but I must decrease

days.title: Living Water
days.focus: Jesus talks with a Samaritan woman at a well, crossing several social barriers, and then heals an official's son from a distance. Notice how the woman's understanding of Jesus grows during the conversation.
days.context: Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility over worship and ancestry, and Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim rather than in Jerusalem. A Jewish teacher speaking alone with a Samaritan woman would have surprised everyone, including his disciples (v. 27).

word.why: This word appears again and again in verses 20–24. The woman asks where to worship; Jesus answers that true worshippers worship 'in spirit and in truth,' moving the question from a place to the heart and to who God is.

questions.q: What does the woman do after her conversation with Jesus (vv. 28–29)?
What does Jesus mean by 'living water,' and why does the woman misunderstand at first?
What 'well' do you keep returning to that never quite satisfies?

checkIn.q: Where did Jesus meet the woman?
What did the nobleman do when Jesus said 'thy son liveth'?
options: He demanded Jesus come with him
He believed the word and went his way

days.title: Healing at Bethesda
days.focus: Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, and because it is the Sabbath, conflict follows. Then Jesus speaks at length about his relationship with the Father and the witnesses who back his claims.
days.context: Archaeologists have found a large pool complex near Jerusalem's Sheep Gate that fits John's description of Bethesda. Verse 4, about an angel stirring the water, is missing from the earliest manuscripts, so some Bibles footnote it.

word.why: Jesus lists his witnesses like evidence in a courtroom: John the Baptist, his own works, the Father, and the scriptures (vv. 31–39). Jewish law required more than one witness, and Jesus offers several.

questions.q: What question does Jesus ask the man by the pool (v. 6)?
What claims does Jesus make about his relationship with the Father in verses 19–27?
Is there an area of your life where you are not sure you want to be made whole?

checkIn.q: How long had the man been ill?
On what day did Jesus heal him?
options: The first day of the week

days.title: The Bread of Life
days.focus: Jesus feeds five thousand, walks on the sea, and then teaches 'I am the bread of life.' Notice how the crowd goes from wanting to make him king to walking away, and how Peter answers when Jesus asks the Twelve if they will leave too.
days.context: The crowd's mention of manna recalls Israel's years in the wilderness. Apart from the resurrection, the feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels.

word.why: The chapter moves from literal loaves to Jesus' claim 'I am the bread of life' (v. 35). Christians differ on how his words about eating his flesh (vv. 51–58) relate to the Lord's Supper, but all agree Jesus presents himself as the true source of life.

questions.q: Why does Jesus say the crowd was seeking him the next day (v. 26)?
What is the difference between the manna in the wilderness and the 'bread of life' Jesus offers?
Peter says, 'Lord, to whom shall we go?' What keeps you following when Jesus' words are hard?

checkIn.q: What did the lad have?
options: Seven loaves and a few fishes
Five barley loaves and two small fishes

checkIn.q: What did Jesus say to the frightened disciples on the sea?
options: It is I; be not afraid

days.title: Rivers of Living Water
days.focus: At the Feast of Tabernacles, people argue about who Jesus is. On the last, great day of the feast, he stands and cries out an invitation. Notice the divided opinions and Nicodemus's cautious defense.
days.context: The Feast of Tabernacles remembered Israel's wilderness years. By Jesus' time it included a daily ceremony of pouring water at the temple.

word.why: 'If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink' (v. 37). At a festival marked by water ceremonies, Jesus presents himself as the answer to thirst, and John explains that he spoke of the Spirit (v. 39).

questions.q: What different opinions about Jesus do people express in this chapter?
What does John say Jesus meant by 'rivers of living water' (v. 39)?
What have you been looking to for refreshment that only God can truly give?

checkIn.q: Which feast was taking place?
Why did the officers return without arresting Jesus?
options: They were afraid of the crowd
Never man spake like this man

days.title: The Truth Shall Make You Free
days.focus: After the story of a woman brought to Jesus for judgment, a sharp debate unfolds in the temple. Jesus calls himself the light of the world, speaks of freedom through truth, and ends with 'Before Abraham was, I am.'
days.context: The account of the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11) does not appear in the earliest manuscripts of John, and many Bibles mark it; many scholars still regard it as an early, genuine tradition about Jesus. 'I am' in verse 58 echoes God's name in Exodus 3:14, which is why the crowd picked up stones.

word.why: 'The truth shall make you free' (v. 32). The listeners protest that they have never been slaves; Jesus means slavery to sin (v. 34) and a freedom only 'the Son' can give (v. 36).

questions.q: What does Jesus say to the woman after her accusers leave?
What kind of slavery is Jesus talking about in verses 31–36?
Where in your life do you most feel the need for the freedom Jesus describes?

checkIn.q: Where did Jesus write with his finger?
How did the crowd react when Jesus said 'Before Abraham was, I am'?
options: They took up stones to cast at him

days.title: Once Blind, Now I See
days.focus: Jesus heals a man blind from birth, and the man is questioned again and again. Watch how his view of Jesus grows (a man, a prophet, one from God, Lord) while the Pharisees grow more certain and less able to see.
days.context: Many people assumed illness or disability was punishment for someone's sin, which is why the disciples ask whose sin caused the blindness. Being put out of the synagogue meant being cut off from one's religious community.

word.why: The word describes the man's physical condition at the start, but by the end Jesus applies it to spiritual blindness (vv. 39–41). The irony is the point: the blind man sees, and those who claim to see are blind.

questions.q: What answer does the man give when he cannot settle the Pharisees' questions (v. 25)?
How does the man's description of Jesus change across the chapter, and why?
What do you know for certain about what Jesus has done for you, even if you cannot answer every question?

checkIn.q: Where did Jesus send the man to wash?
Why did the man's parents avoid answering?
options: They feared being put out of the synagogue

days.title: The Good Shepherd
days.focus: Jesus contrasts himself with thieves and hired hands, calling himself both the door and the good shepherd. Notice what the shepherd does for the sheep, and how the chapter ends with another attempt to stone him.
days.context: Sheep were often kept in walled pens at night, and a flock knew its own shepherd's voice. The Feast of Dedication (v. 22), today called Hanukkah, celebrated the rededication of the temple in the second century BC.

word.why: Israel's leaders were often called shepherds, and God himself is a shepherd in Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34. Jesus claims to be 'the good shepherd' who 'giveth his life for the sheep' (v. 11).

questions.q: What does the good shepherd do that the hireling does not?
Why did Jesus' words 'I and my Father are one' (v. 30) provoke such a strong reaction?
How do you recognize the shepherd's voice among all the other voices in your life?

checkIn.q: What does the good shepherd give for the sheep?
Which feast was taking place in winter?

days.title: Lazarus, Come Forth
days.focus: Jesus delays, Lazarus dies, and Martha and Mary each meet Jesus with the same words. Jesus weeps, then calls Lazarus out of the tomb. Notice the mixed responses, ending with a plot to kill Jesus.
days.context: Bethany was about two miles from Jerusalem (v. 18), close to the city and the authorities. By the fourth day there could be no doubt Lazarus was dead, as Martha's warning about the smell makes plain.

word.why: Martha believes in the resurrection 'at the last day' (v. 24). Jesus answers, 'I am the resurrection, and the life' (v. 25), tying resurrection not only to a future day but to the person standing in front of her.

questions.q: What does Martha say she believes in verse 27?
Why might Jesus weep when he knows he is about to raise Lazarus?
Where do you need Jesus to be 'the resurrection, and the life' now, and not only at the last day?

checkIn.q: How long had Lazarus been in the grave when Jesus arrived?
Who said it was expedient that one man should die for the people?

days.title: The Hour Is Come
days.focus: Mary anoints Jesus, crowds welcome him into Jerusalem, and when some Greeks ask to see him, Jesus announces that 'the hour is come.' Notice the image of a grain of wheat and the chapter's closing summary of belief and unbelief.
days.context: Spikenard was an expensive imported perfume, and three hundred pence was close to a year's wages for a laborer. Palm branches were a symbol of national celebration and victory.

word.why: Jesus says 'The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified' (v. 23) and then speaks of a seed falling into the ground and dying. In John, Jesus' glory is revealed most of all in the cross.

questions.q: What did Judas say should have been done with the ointment, and what does John say was his real motive?
What does the grain of wheat (v. 24) teach about Jesus' death and about following him?
Is there something you are holding tightly that the grain-of-wheat image challenges?

checkIn.q: What did Jesus ride into Jerusalem?
Who came to Philip asking to see Jesus?

days.title: He Washed Their Feet
days.focus: On the night before his death, Jesus washes his disciples' feet, predicts his betrayal, gives a new commandment, and warns Peter of his denial. Notice how John frames everything with Jesus' love 'unto the end' (v. 1).
days.context: People walked dusty roads in sandals, and washing feet was a lowly job usually left to servants. 'The disciple whom Jesus loved' appears here for the first time; tradition has identified him as John.

word.why: Jesus washes their feet (v. 5) and tells Peter, 'If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me' (v. 8). The act pictures cleansing and sets an example: 'ye also ought to wash one another's feet' (v. 14).

questions.q: What does Jesus say will show everyone that his followers are his disciples (v. 35)?
Why does Peter first refuse and then ask to be washed all over? What is Jesus teaching him?
Whose feet would be hardest for you to wash, and why?

checkIn.q: What did Jesus give Judas before he went out?
How many times did Jesus say Peter would deny him before the cock crowed?

days.title: Let Not Your Heart Be Troubled
days.focus: Jesus comforts his anxious disciples with promises: a place prepared, a way to the Father, another Comforter, and his peace. Notice the questions asked by Thomas, Philip, and Judas (not Iscariot), and how Jesus answers each.
days.context: Chapters 13–17 are often called the Farewell Discourse, spoken the night before Jesus' death. 'Mansions' in 1611 English meant dwelling places, not grand houses.

word.why: This word appears in verse 2 ('many mansions') and again in verse 23 ('we will come unto him, and make our abode with him'). The future home with the Father and God's present dwelling with believers are described with the same word.

questions.q: How does Jesus answer when Thomas says 'we know not whither thou goest'?
What does Jesus promise about 'another Comforter' in verses 16–17 and 26?
What is troubling your heart right now?

checkIn.q: Who asked Jesus to 'shew us the Father'?
What does Jesus say he leaves with his disciples?

days.title: Abide in Me
days.focus: Jesus pictures himself as the vine and his disciples as branches. Notice how often 'abide' repeats, how love and obedience are tied together, and the warning that the world will hate his followers.
days.context: Israel was often pictured as God's vine in the Old Testament (Psalm 80, Isaiah 5). Vinedressers prune healthy branches so they will bear more fruit.

word.why: This word appears again and again in verses 4–10. It describes not a one-time decision but an ongoing staying-connected, the way a branch stays joined to the vine to live and bear fruit.

questions.q: What does Jesus say happens to branches that do not abide in him?
What does it mean to 'abide' in Jesus, based on verses 7–10?
What helps you stay connected to Jesus from day to day, and what pulls you away?

checkIn.q: Who is the husbandman?
What does Jesus call his disciples instead of servants?

days.title: Sorrow Turned to Joy
days.focus: Jesus explains why it is better for him to go: the Comforter will come. Notice the picture of a woman in labor, sorrow that turns to joy, and the final words, 'I have overcome the world.'
days.context: Jesus' warning that his followers would be put out of synagogues (v. 2) reflects what many early Jewish believers in Jesus experienced.

word.why: The word describes someone called alongside to help, sometimes as an advocate in court. Jesus says it is 'expedient' for him to go so that the Comforter will come (v. 7), who will convict the world and guide believers into truth.

questions.q: What image does Jesus use in verse 21 for sorrow turning to joy?
Why would it be better for the disciples that Jesus goes away?
Where do you most need to hear 'be of good cheer; I have overcome the world'?

checkIn.q: What does Jesus say the Spirit of truth will do?
How does Jesus end this chapter?

days.title: Jesus Prays for Us
days.focus: Jesus prays for himself, for his disciples, and for all who will believe through their word. Notice what he asks for: glory, protection, holiness, and unity.
days.context: This chapter is often called the High Priestly Prayer because Jesus intercedes for his people like a priest. He prays it just before going out to the garden where he will be arrested.

word.meaning: to sanctify, to make holy, to set apart
word.why: 'Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth' (v. 17), and 'for their sakes I sanctify myself' (v. 19). To sanctify is to set apart for God; Jesus sets himself apart for the cross so his people can be set apart for God.

questions.q: How does Jesus define eternal life in verse 3?
Why does Jesus connect his followers' unity with the world believing (v. 21)?
Jesus prayed for 'them also which shall believe on me through their word' (v. 20). What does it mean to you that he prayed for you?

checkIn.q: According to verse 3, what is eternal life?
options: To know the only true God and Jesus Christ

checkIn.q: Besides his disciples, for whom does Jesus pray?
options: Those who will believe through their word

days.title: What Is Truth?
days.focus: Jesus is arrested in a garden, questioned by Annas, denied by Peter, and brought before Pilate. Notice Jesus' calm control throughout, and Pilate's question, 'What is truth?'
days.context: Annas was a former high priest and father-in-law of the current high priest, Caiaphas, and still powerful behind the scenes. Under Roman rule the Jewish council could not carry out an execution, so they brought Jesus to the Roman governor.

word.why: Jesus says he came 'to bear witness unto the truth' (v. 37). Pilate asks, 'What is truth?' (v. 38) and walks out without waiting for an answer, while the one who called himself 'the truth' (14:6) stands before him.

questions.q: What happened when Jesus said 'I am he' in the garden (v. 6)?
What does Jesus mean when he says his kingdom is 'not of this world' (v. 36)?
Peter denied Jesus in a moment of fear. Where are you most tempted to hide your connection to him?

checkIn.q: Whose ear did Peter cut off?
Whom did the crowd ask Pilate to release?

days.title: It Is Finished
days.focus: Pilate hands Jesus over, and he is crucified, dies, and is buried. Notice the scriptures John says were fulfilled, Jesus' care for his mother, and the two secret disciples who bury him.
days.context: The title on the cross was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, so anyone passing by could read it. Bodies were taken down before the Sabbath because leaving them on a cross over a holy day was considered defiling.

word.meaning: to finish, to complete, to accomplish
word.why: Jesus' last word in John is 'It is finished' (v. 30). It is a cry of completion, not defeat: the work the Father gave him to do is done (compare 17:4).

questions.q: What did Jesus say to his mother and to the disciple he loved?
Why do you think John points out the scriptures fulfilled in verses 24, 28, and 36–37?
What does 'It is finished' mean for something you have been trying to complete on your own?

checkIn.q: In what languages was the title on the cross written?
Who brought myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial?

days.title: My Lord and My God
days.focus: The tomb is empty, Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus, and the disciples, then Thomas, see him. Notice how each person comes to believe differently, and read John's purpose statement at the end.
days.context: In that culture a woman's testimony was often given less weight, yet all four Gospels name women as the first witnesses of the empty tomb.

word.why: John states his purpose: 'that ye might believe' (v. 31). This verb runs through the whole Gospel, and this chapter shows people coming to believe in different ways: at an empty tomb, by hearing a name, by seeing wounds.

questions.q: When did Mary recognize Jesus?
What does Jesus mean by 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' (v. 29)?
Which person in this chapter is most like you in the way you have come to faith?

checkIn.q: Who came to the tomb early, while it was still dark?
What did Thomas say when he saw Jesus?

days.title: Lovest Thou Me?
days.focus: Back in Galilee, the risen Jesus provides a great catch of fish and cooks breakfast on the shore. Then he asks Peter three times, 'Lovest thou me?' Notice what he tells Peter to do after each answer.
days.context: Jesus' 'fire of coals' (v. 9) uses the same rare Greek word as the fire where Peter denied him (18:18); these are the only two places it appears in the New Testament. Peter's three answers echo his three denials.

word.why: Jesus asks 'lovest thou me?' using agapao twice and phileo the third time, while Peter answers with phileo each time. Some readers see a meaningful difference and others see simple variation, since John uses both words for the same love; either way, three questions answer three denials.

questions.q: What does Jesus tell Peter to do after each of his answers?
Why might Jesus ask Peter the same question three times?
If Jesus asked you 'lovest thou me?' today, how would you answer?

checkIn.q: How many fish were in the net?
options: An hundred and fifty and three

checkIn.q: What did Jesus tell Peter to do?

leader.intro: This study meets three times, once after each week of seven chapters. Plan 60–75 minutes: 10 minutes to settle in, 45 minutes of discussion, and 10–15 minutes of prayer. A week of John is a lot of reading, so expect that some people will be behind; invite them to come anyway, and choose one or two scenes per session to read aloud together so everyone has the text fresh. John is full of 'I am' sayings and signs; a simple running list on a whiteboard or shared note can help the group see the pattern grow over three weeks.

sessions.title: Signs and First Encounters
sessions.opening: Think of a first meeting that changed the course of your life. What made it memorable?
discussion: John 1 gives Jesus many titles. Which ones stood out to you, and what does each say about him?
John calls Jesus' miracles 'signs.' What do the signs in chapters 2, 4, 5, and 6 point to?
Compare Nicodemus (ch. 3) and the Samaritan woman (ch. 4). How are they different, and how does Jesus meet each one?
In chapter 5, Jesus lists witnesses to who he is. Why do you think John cares so much about testimony?
In chapter 6, many followers leave. What made Jesus' words so hard to accept, and why did Peter stay?
In chapter 7, people are divided about Jesus. What reasons do they give for their opinions?
Which encounter this week do you most identify with, and why?
sessions.notes: John was likely the last Gospel written, and it includes much material the others don't, such as Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, and long teaching sections. John states his purpose in 20:31, so it can help to read that verse aloud at the start: everything in the book is meant to help readers believe. The 'signs' are a key thread; seven are commonly counted (water to wine, the official's son, the man at the pool, the feeding, walking on water, the man born blind, Lazarus), though people count them differently. John 3:16 is so familiar that groups can skip past it; it may help to read verses 14–21 together so its context (the bronze serpent, light and darkness) comes through. John 6:51-58 is understood differently across Christian traditions, especially regarding the Lord's Supper; name that respectfully and focus on what everyone agrees on, that Jesus is the true source of life. People sometimes ask about the temple clearing appearing early in John; scholars differ on whether there were two events or whether John arranged it by theme, and either view is held by thoughtful Christians.
sessions.prayer: Thank God for the ways Jesus has met each of you, and pray for someone you know who is still asking questions like Nicodemus.

sessions.title: Light, Life, and the Shepherd
sessions.opening: When have you been unable to see something that was obvious to someone else?
discussion: In chapter 8, Jesus says the truth will make people free. What kind of freedom does he mean, and why did his listeners resist it?
Trace how the blind man's understanding of Jesus grows in chapter 9. What does this teach about spiritual sight?
What does the good shepherd do in chapter 10 that a hired hand would not?
In chapter 11, Jesus weeps at the tomb even though he knows he will raise Lazarus. What does that tell us about him?
What does Jesus mean by a grain of wheat dying to bear fruit (12:24-25)?
Why does Jesus wash the disciples' feet, and what does he expect them to do with that example?
Which promise in chapter 14 do you most need this week?
sessions.notes: Many Bibles mark John 7:53–8:11 because it does not appear in the earliest manuscripts; many scholars think it is a genuine early story about Jesus that found a home here. If someone asks, a brief, calm explanation is enough; it does not change any Christian teaching. In 8:58, 'Before Abraham was, I am' echoes God's name in Exodus 3:14, which explains the violent reaction. In chapter 9, the disciples assume suffering is caused by someone's sin; Jesus rejects that as the explanation here, which can be meaningful for group members carrying illness or disability. Chapter 11 includes the shortest verse in the KJV ('Jesus wept,' 11:35); let the group sit with the fact that Jesus grieves. In chapter 13, groups sometimes discuss whether footwashing should be practiced literally; some churches do so, and others see it as an example of humble service in general. John 14:6 ('I am the way, the truth, and the life') can raise questions about other religions; acknowledge the question honestly and keep the focus on what Jesus is offering his frightened disciples in context.
sessions.prayer: Pray for any in the group carrying grief or loss, and thank Jesus as the good shepherd who knows each one by name.

sessions.title: Farewell, Cross, and Resurrection
sessions.opening: What is a piece of advice or a last word from someone you love that has stayed with you?
discussion: What does it look like to 'abide' in Jesus (ch. 15)? What helps, and what gets in the way?
In chapter 16, Jesus says it is better for the disciples that he leave. Why?
What does Jesus pray for in chapter 17? What stands out to you about his prayer for future believers?
How does Jesus act during his arrest and trials in chapter 18? What does that show about him?
What is 'finished' when Jesus says 'It is finished' (19:30)?
Mary, the beloved disciple, and Thomas each come to believe in different ways in chapter 20. Which way is closest to your own story?
In chapter 21, how does Jesus restore Peter? What does this teach about failure and forgiveness?
sessions.notes: Chapters 13–17 are Jesus' farewell, and chapter 17 is often called the High Priestly Prayer; consider reading part of it aloud slowly. John's account of the cross emphasizes Jesus' control and the fulfillment of scripture more than his agony, so groups that know the other Gospels may notice a different tone. John says the crucifixion took place on 'the preparation of the passover' (19:14), and many readers see significance in Jesus dying around the time Passover lambs were prepared; the other Gospels describe the Last Supper as a Passover meal, and scholars have proposed different ways to fit the timelines together. In chapter 21, much has been written on the two Greek words for love (agapao and phileo) in Peter's restoration; some see a meaningful difference and others think John uses them interchangeably, so do not let the group get stuck there. The main point is that three questions answer three denials, and Peter is given work to do. End the series by reading 20:30-31 again and asking how the group has seen Jesus differently over three weeks.
sessions.prayer: Thank God for the finished work of Christ, and pray for one another to abide in him and to feed his sheep.
